Fertilised eggs of the lugworm Arenicola marina are remarkably small, with an average diameter of 0.02 centimeters , a dimension that places them among the smaller free-spawned ova of intertidal polychaetes. At the moment of syngamy, the resulting zygote has a minimal wet weight calculated at 0.00000478 grams [Ww0 = 0.00000478 grams], reflecting the limited maternal provisioning provided to the embryo. Following fecundation and subsequent cleavage, the rapidly developing embryo progresses through the blastula and gastrula stages while still reliant upon its endogenous yolk reserves. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the transition from a free-swimming trochophore larva to a newly settled juvenile, defined here as the onset of a benthic existence and the beginning of morphological change, occurs after approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days]. This developmental schedule is notably temperature-sensitive and appears to accelerate markedly under the warmer conditions typical of shallow intertidal pools during summer months, though the precise thermal optimum for early ontogeny remains incompletely resolved.

The trochophore larva of Arenicola marina first becomes distinguishable as a free-swimming, exogenously feeding organism at a relatively early stage of development. In cultures held at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], these actively growing, planktonic larvae are regularly observed after only 7 days  post-fertilisation. At this point, the larva measures approximately 0.025 centimeters  in total length, a size that allows it to exploit the microbial food web of the water column through cilia-driven feeding. This initial larval phase is brief compared to the total duration of pelagic life, yet it represents a critical window during which the larva must accumulate sufficient resources to support the profound body plan reorganisation that characterises subsequent metamorphosis. The transition from the early, pre-metamorphic trochophore to the later metatrochophore stage is accompanied by the gradual elaboration of the larval feeding apparatus and the incipient development of the juvenile body segments, setting the stage for the eventual settlement and benthic recruitment event that will define the post-larval phase.

As the trochophore larva continues its pelagic existence, it undergoes a significant allometric shift that culminates in the metamorphic climax and the emergence of a post-larval juvenile worm. The total length of the larva at the moment of metamorphosis has been measured at 0.89 centimeters , representing a substantial increase in size from the earlier trochophore stage. This larval-juvenile transition is temperature-dependent and, in cultures maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the entire process from fertilisation through to the completion of morphological transformation takes approximately 78 days . Upon settlement, the newly recruited juvenile worm bears little resemblance to the pelagic larva it once was, having gained the segmented body plan and the burrowing apparatus that will define its infaunal adult life. The post-metamorphic juvenile is already capable of constructing the characteristic U-shaped burrows in soft sediments, and it begins to feed on the organic matter present in the sediment, marking a complete shift from the planktotrophic feeding mode of its larval predecessor.

Following settlement and recruitment into the benthos, the growing juvenile worm embarks on a prolonged period of somatic growth and segment addition that gradually transforms it into a reproductively competent adult. The trunk length, measured from the anterior to the posterior end of the trunk region, can eventually reach a maximum of 34 centimeters  in particularly large, senescent individuals. The onset of gametogenesis and the attainment of reproductive maturity are, however, achieved considerably earlier. The smallest mature individual recorded in field surveys possessed a trunk length of 2.5 centimeters , indicating that sexual maturation can occur at a relatively modest body size. In terms of chronological age, first reproduction in this species is estimated to occur at approximately 547.5 days after hatching [tR = approximately 547.5 days after hatching] at 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This value, while providing a useful benchmark, must be regarded as tentative, as it is derived from a single population and may not reflect the full range of intraspecific variation across the species' geographic distribution.

Field records and laboratory observations together indicate that Arenicola marina possesses a maximum lifespan that, while probably underestimated in many studies, has been pegged at approximately 2190 days [am = approximately 2190 days] when individuals are maintained at around 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. This relatively extended longevity for a burrowing polychaete may be linked to the species' low metabolic demands and its occupation of a stable, albeit intertidally variable, sedimentary habitat. At birth, the newly settled juvenile begins its benthic life with a total body length of just 0.08 centimeters [Lb = 0.08 centimeters], a diminutive size that makes it vulnerable to a host of epibenthic predators and physical disturbance from tidal action. Survivorship during this early benthic phase is consequently thought to be low, with high mortality acting as a major bottleneck in the species' demography. The interplay between temperature, food availability, and local sediment characteristics ultimately governs the pace at which these worms progress from the vulnerable juvenile stage to the reproductively active adult phase, thereby shaping population dynamics across the European intertidal zone.
